Original post: Thought this would be nice to see what classes might be interesting for people not in your major to take. Feel free to share favorite professors or clubs/opportunities too.

A student wrote that Dr. Zinser's social and emotional learning lab was a positive experience. The student said people in the lab were welcoming and the environment felt like home. They described joining as a freshman, being mentored, and being allowed to work at their own pace.

. They described joining as a freshman, being mentored, and being allowed to work at their own pace.

A computer science major wrote that any course can be interesting if a student is willing to put in effort and learn. They suggested CS 151/301 for theory-oriented students, CS 251/342 for hands-on programming, and CS 261 for machine code or assembly. The student also mentioned that they later received a research spot in machine learning with Professor McCarty.

In a follow-up, the same student said they took CS 151 with McCarty, did well, went to office hours, and became known to the professor. They then contacted him after finals and said that after taking CS 251 and a statistics class, students could try to get themselves known to a professor and then follow up by email. They described this as showing dedication and seriousness.

Original post: The original post was deleted, but the discussion focused on whether a high school student could get research experience in or near UIC labs.

One former graduate student said a high school student would need to find a lab where the work does not require much background knowledge. They explained that some labs have preparatory work or data collection work, but many labs require background knowledge or relevant courses. The same commenter said that, in their lab, even undergraduates were not accepted often because the lab work required later coursework.

eir lab, even undergraduates were not accepted often because the lab work required later coursework.

Another commenter suggested emailing every professor in the department where the student is interested in doing research. They said they once emailed about 40 professors, received about 15 replies, got 3 interviews, and ended up with 2 research labs.

A commenter warned against sending generic emails. They said a generic letter is a red flag because it suggests the student is not truly interested in the professor's work. They recommended identifying researchers whose work is personally interesting, explaining why the work is interesting, and showing enthusiasm for that specific project.

Another commenter said high school students should be patient and focus on doing well in school first. They said more research resources would be available later in university or community college.

irst. They said more research resources would be available later in university or community college.

A final commenter said research may be possible if the student has relevant programming skills such as Python, Rust, C, or C++. They recommended preparing a resume and sending it to professors in ECE or Computer Science, but emphasized that students must be serious and committed.

UIC Artificial Intelligence Laboratory Projects page.

Project: Gary-Chicago-Milwaukee corridor transportation information. The GCM corridor is described as one of four Priority Corridors in the United States. The corridor includes the greater metropolitan areas of Gary, Chicago, and Milwaukee, plus portions of southeast Wisconsin, northeast Illinois, and northwest Indiana. The goal of the project is to improve mobility by better managing transportation systems instead of simply building new roads. The project focuses on operational testbeds for intelligent transportation systems, regional traffic improvement, public awareness, institutional relationships, and testing new technologies.

al traffic improvement, public awareness, institutional relationships, and testing new technologies.

Project: Data mining for manufacturing and design processes. This project focuses on large-scale datasets with numeric and nominal attributes. The goal is to discover and predict hidden patterns or relationships among data attributes that affect manufacturing and production quality. The techniques include decision trees, decision rules, neural networks, and traditional machine learning methods. The project also investigates adaptive evolutionary computational methods for complex problems. One approach uses Gene Expression Programming, a genetic-algorithm-family method that evolves computer programs and predicts mathematical functions from experimental data. Experiments included multi-category pattern classification problems.

Project: Text summarization. This project studies natural language processing and machine learning methods for summarization. The page explains that people face information overload from emails, news headlines, traffic reports, scientific articles, browsing webpages, and other sources. Automated text summarization is described as a way to reduce information overload and help users identify important information.

The Database and Mobile Computing Laboratory page describes the Moving Objects Databases project. The project is called Databases For MovIng Objects tracking, abbreviated DOMINO. It develops a prototype database system for tracking mobile units.

The project was partly supported by NSF grants 0326284, 0513736, and 0209190. The page names Ouri Wolfson as the project director. Other participants include graduate student Damian Roqueiro, Venkata Kumar Srinivasan, Leon Stenneth, Fatemeh Vafae, Mayia Arun, Lei Zhang, and research scientist Dr. Bo Xu.

The page links to an overview paper titled Moving Objects Information Management: The Database Challenge, from the Proceedings of the 5th Workshop on Next Generation Information Technologies and Systems in 2002. The project relates to location management, moving objects information management, mobile computing, database systems, and tracking mobile units.

Established in 1973, the Electronic Visualization Laboratory, or EVL, is an interdisciplinary research laboratory in the UIC College of Engineering's Computer Science department. EVL specializes in collaborative visualization, virtual reality, visual data science, and advanced computing and networking infrastructure.

EVL enables scientists and engineers to manage data scale and complexity by creating information visualizations of multidimensional and multivariate data, exploring 3D immersive worlds, juxtaposing related yet heterogeneous 2D and 3D datasets, accessing computer infrastructure for machine learning, and moving large datasets over high-speed networks.

ng computer infrastructure for machine learning, and moving large datasets over high-speed networks.

EVL has a long history of work in real-time interactive graphics, videogame technology, scientific visualization, advanced virtual reality, and high-speed networking infrastructure. The lab is known for inventions including the CAVE virtual reality environment, the ImmersaDesk, OptIPortal, SAGE scalable adaptive graphics environment, and the Continuum Collaborative Smart Space.

EVL's current work includes hardware and software technologies such as the CAVE2 hybrid-reality environment, SAGE2 scalable amplified group environment, and SAGE3 smart amplified group environment. The lab continues to expand in scientific visualization, information visualization, visual analytics, and collaborative research.

n scientific visualization, information visualization, visual analytics, and collaborative research.

EVL collaborates with computational scientists and application scientists in academia, government, and industry. EVL faculty, staff, and students form interdisciplinary teams to create useful and usable visualization and virtual-reality tools connected to remote data stores and colleagues over high-speed networks. EVL maintains a distinguished publication record, with students, faculty, and staff publishing in major journals and conferences worldwide.
